zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Used only as a secondary identification aid, not as a diplomatic transcription. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

lines.note: Continues the previous page's ichi-i suru definition: becoming one body with someone in will or intention. Corpo is actual body text here, unlike the catchword on f259.
This ichii is a fruit compared with acorns. The internal hyphen separates the vowels in the print; no botanical species is inferred from the brief comparison.
Ichiichi means each thing individually. The example reads Ichiichini, including the second i and final ni; it is not the OCR's divided Ichichin-, and the verb follows below.
Mooshi hiraku means explaining or setting forth each matter individually. The Portuguese begins the same explanation with em par-, continued as particular.
Ticular completes particular. The short row closes the item-by-item explanation and remains a distinct physical line.

Ichizen is one good deed or virtue, hitotsu no zen. The Japanese jẽ is entirely roman; obra corrects OCR ebra. The preceding bou is retained as the locally u-like printed form rather than silently normalized to boa.
Ichiji is one temple, hitotsu no tera. The Portuguese uses varela and Igreja; the latter begins with a capital I, not OCR lowercase l.
This ichiji is a time or brief interval, hitotsu no toki. The example below demonstrates the 'even for a moment' use rather than an exact modern clock-hour conversion.
The negative example says the speaker does not forget even briefly. The printed fenximo is retained as it stands; the Portuguese eſque- continues into eſqueço below.

runs.text: ço nem por hum breue eſpaço.

lines.note: Ço completes eſqueço, followed by 'not even for a brief space'. This is the Portuguese counterpart of the preceding Japanese negative example.
This ichiji is one matter, hitotsu no koto, glossed hũa couſa. It is a separate homographic entry rather than another temporal example.
Ichijiki is eating once, paraphrased hitotabi shokusu. The scan has Fitotabi, not OCR Fitotebi; the Portuguese describes a fast allowing a single meal.
The fast permits eating only once. The example has the visibly separated Ichijiq uo, with an abbreviated or defective final stem; no expected i is invented before the object particle.

runs.text: Iejuar comendo hũa ſoo vez no dia.

lines.note: The translation explicitly describes fasting by eating only once in the day. It explains the preceding example without repairing its unusual printed Japanese spelling.
Ichijitsu is solid or substantial truth. The closing label is Bup., indicating Buddhist terminology, not OCR Buo; it is upright in the scan.
Ichijoo is one fortress, hitotsu no shiro. The visible o restores fortaleza from OCR frtaleza, while the headword's caron remains unchanged.
Ichiju is one and the same tree, hitotsu no ki. The colon introduces the dictionary's restriction on the contexts in which the expression is used.

runs.text: ſempre ſe vſa em compoſição de outras pala-

lines.note: The word is said always to occur in combination with other words. Pala- continues as palauras on the next physical row.
Ichiju no kage ni yoru means approaching or taking shelter in the same tree's shade. The Portuguese Che- begins chegarſe across the line break.

runs.text: garſe à ſombra da meſma aruore.

lines.note: Garſe completes chegarſe, followed by the shade of the same tree. This closes the illustrative construction, without inserting a further proverbial interpretation.
Ichimegasa names broad hats worn by women. The faint i after Ich is retained from compatible traces and the headword's form; the Portuguese molheres is not modernized.
Ichimei is life, equated with inochi. The gloss also covers the period for which a person lives, continued below.
Viue completes the life-span gloss, and ichimei no aida illustrates it. The example stays on its own physical row after the Portuguese continuation.
Ichimen and the alternative adverb ichimenni are paraphrased hitotsu omote. The second form is visibly lowercase, unlike OCR Ichimenni; l is the alternative marker.
The Portuguese gives one appearance or manner. Shigojuu begins the example of forty or fifty people; the scan does not support the OCR's internal space in Xigojǔ.
Nin completes the people count. Ichimenni zararito naoru describes the group turning or arranging themselves alike; Quarẽta begins the numerical Portuguese translation.

runs.text: ou cincoẽta ſe virarão todos de hũa maneira.

lines.note: The forty or fifty people all turn in the same manner. The worn r restores virarão from OCR vira ão; the printed nasal abbreviations in the number and article remain unchanged.
Ichimi is one body or union. The example ichimi ni naru starts here and continues onto the next line; this is the social-unity sense.
Ni naru completes 'become one body'. The following Itẽ introduces another sense of ichimi, developed in the next row rather than absorbed into this translation.
The second ichimi is a single ingredient in medicine. The Portuguese material de mezinhas is a substance or ingredient, not a modern material category.
Kusuri ichimi wo kuwayuru means adding another medicinal ingredient. The scan supports cuuayuru rather than OCR cuuayoru; the historical verb form is not replaced with a modern one.
Hum material de mezinha completes the instruction to add one ingredient. This is the final line of the medicine sense, distinct from the following dust-speck entry.
Ichimijin is a speck of dust, hitotsu no chiri. The Portuguese argueiro prepares the figurative sense of an extremely small amount.
The explanatory marker is i, with a comma. Toga ichimijin begins an example denying even the smallest fault; the Japanese remains roman after the Portuguese introduction.
Hodo mo nai completes the emphatic negation. The Portuguese says not to have even a minimal sin, with the noun continuing below.
Peccado completes the translation of toga. The doubled c is preserved rather than modernized.
Ichimyoo is one name, hitotsu no na. The visible caron on the long vowel is retained as the source's notation.
Ichimoo is one hair, hitotsu no ke. The initial I is faint beside the rule but belongs to the headword; no full stop is added after cabelo where the print proceeds to the paragraph marker.
The figurative extension is a very small thing or quantity. This continues the hair entry and does not yet refer to a decimal unit.
Ichimoo is defined as a tenth of ichirin. The unit name embedded in Portuguese reads Ichirin, not OCR tibirin; the final Ichi- begins the next, smaller unit across the row break.
Fot completes Ichifot, defined as a tenth of ichimoo. The embedded Ichimô carries a circumflex, not the OCR's grave; the following Ix continues below without an invented hyphen.
Xi completes Ixxi, a tenth of Ichifot. The final letter in the embedded unit is t, not OCR i; Ichi begins the next unit and remains unhyphenated as printed.

Mi completes Ichimi, one tenth of Ixxi. The embedded unit Ixxi remains upright within the italic Portuguese explanation, preserving the visible type contrast; ve begins verá across the row break, with no supplied hyphen.

runs.text: rà mais claramente nas contas do dinheiro,

lines.note: Rà completes verá. The dictionary promises a clearer explanation in the sections on monetary accounts, continuing to weights below.
Peſos and &c. finish the forward reference to accounts and weights. This short line closes the sequence of fractional units.
This ichimoo means a blind person. Its caron is retained and distinguishes the printed form from the preceding circumflexed hair and fractional-unit headwords.
Ichimoku is one silence or a moment of silence. The scan has i in the headword and long ſ in ſilencio, not OCR Ichumocu or filencio; Banguen begins the maxim continued in column 2.
This completes the maxim begun with Banguen: even many words do not equal silence. The final Xix. is a citation label with a full stop, not the OCR's apparent trailing hyphen.

runs.text: Mais val calar, que falar muitas boas couſas

lines.note: The Portuguese says it is better to be silent than to say many good things. The last word reads couſas, with final s, not OCR couſao; the thought continues on the next row.
The continuation adds that the words are appropriate or to the point. Apropoſito is printed as one word; the OCR's apropoſteo misidentifies the final syllables.
This ichimon denotes a family, with Fitotçuno cado as the Japanese explanatory synonym. Keep the synonym in roman rather than treating it as Japanese embedded within Portuguese.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Hũa congregação de gẽte como re-

lines.note: A second sense is a congregation of people, illustrated by religious communities. The abbreviated gẽte and the line-final re- are visible and retained.
Ligioſos completes religioſos: members of the same religious order. The medial character in meſma is long s, not j; the paragraph sign introduces a Japanese example split after qe-.
Zocu completes qezocu; the example concerns the assembling of a family and its kin. The Portuguese translation begins on this row and continues with familia below.
Familia closes the preceding translation. This is a short indented continuation, not a separate headword or an omitted example.
The new ichimon is one written character. The damaged initial is capital I rather than long s, and letra has a faint but recoverable t; Vt introduces the illiteracy example.

runs.text: O não ſaber nem hũa ſoo letra, co-

lines.note: Futçǔ completes the expression for not understanding a single character. The Japanese cluster is tç rather than OCR rg, and the mark over u is read as a caron; the Portuguese retains ſoo.

runs.text: mo hum ruſtico que não aprendeo aler nem a eſ

lines.note: The definition compares this with an unlettered rustic who has not learned to read or write. Aler is joined as printed; eſ continues below without adding an unsupported line-end hyphen.
Creuer completes eſcreuer, then an equivalent expression describes an illiterate person. Ichimõ has a nasal bar or tilde, not a caron; the damaged mark on futçǔno is read with the preceding futçǔ.
This completes Peſſoa que não ſabe ler, the definition of the preceding Japanese expression. The physical split of Peſ- and ſoa is preserved.

runs.text: Hũa letra que he como hũa riſca

lines.note: Ichimonji is explained as the single written character resembling a horizontal stroke. The wording describes the character's shape rather than introducing a Portuguese technical term.

The example is translated below as a person unable to read even a simple character. The scan has an r-like glyph in xiraru; retain that printed reading rather than silently supplying the contextually expected xiranu.

runs.text: Homem que não ſabe nada de ler, ou

lines.note: No completes mono, followed by the description of a man who knows nothing of reading or writing. Ou continues the coordinated definition on the next physical line.

runs.text: eſcreuer nẽ hũa letra facil q̃ he como hũa riſca.

lines.note: The definition continues: not even a simple character like a single stroke. The scan supports nasal nẽ, hũa without an extra i, and letra rather than OCR ſetra; q̃ remains abbreviated.
Ichimonjini is an adverb meaning straight or along a straight line. The adverbial label remains part of the italic Portuguese explanation.
Direita completes the literal straight-line sense. The next sense is marked Permet., a figurative-use abbreviation; the final glyph is t rather than OCR s, and Recta is retained.
Regularmente completes the figurative definition, meaning regularly or properly. This short indented row belongs to the same adverbial entry.
Ichimot denotes one thing. The final vowel of the Portuguese noun looks like e in this impression; preserve the printed couſe rather than silently regularizing it to couſa.
A second ichimot, explained by Sugureta mono, is a unique or outstanding thing. This is a separate lexical sense, not an accidental duplicate of the previous row.
The definition specifies excellence, with a falcon, horse, and dog as examples. Keep the historical caualo and the printed nasal abbreviations in falcão and cão.
Ichimu is one dream, explained by Fitotçuno yume. The synonym has no extra i after çu; the Portuguese definition confirms the dream sense.
The example compares transient life with waking from a dream. The damaged beginning of ſamuruga remains compatible with the supplied reading; the visible final stop after gotoxi is restored.

runs.text: O mundo acabaſe como hum ſonho.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the example as the world ending like a dream. Acabaſe stays joined, retaining the source spelling rather than adding a modern hyphen.
This ichinen is a single thought. The short definition is complete on its own row, before a homophonous but distinct entry.
The second ichinen means one year. The Portuguese is Hum anno, with double n, not the OCR's Humanrio; it is distinct from the preceding thought sense.
Ichinho is defined as one woman. The unusual romanization is retained as printed rather than replacing it with a modern Japanese reading.

runs.text: Hum dia, ou todo o dia. Vt,

lines.note: Ichinichi means one day or the whole day. The line-final Ichi starts the example, whose second component nichi continues below without a supplied hyphen.
Nichi completes Ichinichi; xincu ſuru is translated as working all day. Trabalhar has ra, not the OCR's oa in Toabalhar.
Ichinin is an act of forbearance or patience. Vt introduces a maxim that continues on the next row; this is not the homophonous expression for one person.
The maxim contrasts many battles and victories with one act of patience. The second compound has the faint i of fiacuxômo; the first remains Fiacuxen, and the final xicaji is not modernized.

runs.text: Mais val hũa vez ter paciencia que alcançar

lines.note: The translation says that a single act of patience is worth more than winning victories. Alcançar ends in ar rather than the OCR's or; hũa is retained with its nasal abbreviation.
This completes the comparison with many victories in war. The row is an indented continuation of the maxim's Portuguese translation.
Ichinoo is an art or skill, glossed by Fitotçuno vaza. The worn t and the letters of vaza are recoverable; the paragraph example begins with capital I- rather than lowercase l-.
Chinôuo completes Ichinôuo, followed by motta fito, a person possessing a skill. The stem contains n, not OCR u; al- begins algũa in the Portuguese translation.
The translation specifies possessing an art or ability to an eminent degree. Algũa remains split across the physical rows, with the printed nasal sign preserved here.
Ichino tai denotes the principal woman or the head among the women of a household. The entry's Japanese spacing is retained and its definition continues below.

runs.text: as outras em caſa dalgum Yacata, ou ſenhor

lines.note: The household belongs to a Yacata or great lord. Yacata is a Japanese title embedded in the Portuguese sentence; its whole word is kept with the italic explanation rather than the OCR's isolated roman Y.
Grande completes ſenhor grande, closing the definition of the principal woman. This single-word row is retained as an indented body continuation.

runs.text: Braço dos ombros tee o cotouelo.

lines.note: Ichino vde is the upper arm, from the shoulder to the elbow. The source appears to print tee with two e letters; preserve that historical form rather than reducing it to modern até or OCR te.

runs.text: O ſegundo oßo que eſta da ponta

lines.note: Ichino zzu is defined by the position of a bone below the top of the spine. The doubled z and the oßo ligature are retained rather than regularized.

runs.text: do eſpinhaço pera baixo entre os ombros.

lines.note: The definition locates that bone down from the end of the spine, between the shoulders. Keep the old directional wording pera baixo and the spelling eſpinhaço.

runs.text: Cair, ou deſfalecer hũa vez. Vt,

lines.note: Ichiracu means to fall or decline once. Vt introduces the example on the next row; this entry continues normally above the separate bottom catchword.
The Japanese juxtaposes flourishing and decline as things occurring before one's eyes. The Portuguese begins Não ha and continues with its object below; no additional accent is supplied.
The final row completes the statement that no prosperity lasts long. Proſperidade has the visible eri sequence and no nasal abbreviation; dure and muito replace the OCR's cure and mito.
